concepts.decision: Put security decisions and evidence in each applicable phase and feed operational results into subsequent work.
concepts.definition: The software development life cycle: coordinated phases from initiation and requirements through design, build, test, deployment, operation, and retirement.
concepts.failureExample: A project that ends controls at deployment leaves patching, monitoring, revocation, and disposal unmanaged.
concepts.label: Sdlc

concepts.decision: Define requirements from asset value, threat, compliance, privacy, resilience, and owner needs, then trace them to evidence.
concepts.definition: Testable security outcomes that constrain the product before design and implementation.
concepts.failureExample: A vague “secure API” requirement gives testers no criterion for access or audit behavior.
concepts.label: Security Requirements

concepts.decision: Use it at design and revisit it after material changes or operational evidence changes assumptions.
concepts.definition: Attacker-oriented analysis of system boundaries, assets, entry points, abuse cases, and control assumptions.
concepts.failureExample: An added partner integration can create replay/spoofing paths that the original model never assessed.
concepts.label: Threat Modeling

concepts.decision: Integrate security at initiation, requirements, design, test, and release gates; manage authorized rework when requirements change.
concepts.definition: A phased SDLC with formal baselines and milestone approvals before proceeding.
concepts.failureExample: A final-only security review may uncover an architectural flaw after the baseline is costly to change.
concepts.label: Waterfall

concepts.decision: Include security stories, acceptance criteria, threat-model updates, and tests in each increment.
concepts.definition: Iterative lifecycle delivery in small, collaborative increments that can incorporate frequent feedback.
concepts.failureExample: Deferring security stories to a final sprint recreates a late hardening phase.
concepts.label: Agile

concepts.decision: Use operational telemetry and ownership to inform delivery decisions, while keeping security evidence and release accountability.
concepts.definition: An approach that connects development and operations for rapid, reliable delivery and feedback.
concepts.failureExample: Fast automation without monitored rollback can spread a faulty configuration rapidly.
concepts.label: Devops

concepts.decision: Use early automated checks where reliable, with accountable human review for risk, architecture, exceptions, and incident learning.
concepts.definition: Integration of security practices, people, and suitable automation into development and operations workflows.
concepts.failureExample: A pipeline can pass static checks while the deployed authorization configuration is wrong.
concepts.label: Devsecops

concepts.decision: Apply it to discover issues before implementation while retaining runtime monitoring and feedback; it does not mean “only early security.”
concepts.definition: Moving security analysis, requirements, design review, and defect discovery earlier in the lifecycle where change is cheaper and more influential.
concepts.failureExample: Treating shift-left as a substitute for production monitoring misses deployed configuration and abuse behavior.
concepts.label: Shift Left

misconceptions.claim: Shift-left means security is finished before deployment.
misconceptions.correction: Early prevention is valuable, but runtime monitoring, patching, incident response, and retirement remain necessary.

outcome: Place security activities and decision gates across an SDLC and explain how methodology affects timing, ownership, and evidence.

sections.body: Requirements should express security, privacy, resilience, and compliance needs; design should model threats, trust boundaries, and controls; implementation should use secure standards and review; testing should challenge abuse cases and controls; deployment should preserve configuration and provenance; operations should monitor, patch, respond, and learn; retirement should revoke access and dispose of data and secrets.
keyPoints: Earlier discovery usually lowers the cost and disruption of correction.
Security ownership follows the product and system lifecycle.
Trace requirements to design, code, tests, and operational evidence.
sections.title: Build security into each phase

sections.body: Waterfall emphasizes phase gates and formal baselines; iterative and agile methods deliver smaller increments; DevOps integrates development and operations; DevSecOps adds security collaboration and automation. No method makes security automatic: define acceptance criteria, threat-model changes, protect pipelines, and keep feedback fast enough to influence delivery.
keyPoints: Security activities can be continuous even when governance gates remain formal.
Automation supports consistency but does not replace judgment.
Speed-to-market pressure must be balanced with risk and evidence.
sections.title: Adapt to delivery method
